blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-security-1 (API tokens are stored in clear in the database) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-security-2 (The middleware logs the Authorization header, writing every token to the logs) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
The `api_tokens` table holds `user_id`, `token` and `created_at`; the
middleware looks a request's token up with `WHERE token = $1`. Storing the
token as given keeps the lookup a simple indexed equality.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Tokens are stored as given
findings.recommendation: Store only a hash of the token (SHA-256 of the 32 random bytes is enough for a high-entropy secret; no bcrypt needed) in a `token_hash` column with a unique index, and look the request's token up with `WHERE token_hash = $1` after hashing it — the lookup stays a simple indexed equality, so the stated reason for storing the token as given does not hold. Scenario that fails today: anyone who reads the `api_tokens` table — a database backup, a read replica, an SQL injection elsewhere in the service, a support operator with read access — gets every user's live bearer credential and can call the API as any user (CWE-312 / CWE-256). Unlike `users.password_hash`, which the design already keeps hashed with bcrypt, these tokens are directly usable. Update the "Alternatives considered" line, which wrongly states there is none, and task 1.1/1.2 to test that the stored value is not the token.
findings.title: API tokens are stored in clear in the database

findings.evidence:
method, path and headers at `info` level, including `Authorization`, so
support can see which token an integration sent.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Every request is logged with its headers
findings.recommendation: Never log the `Authorization` header (nor `Cookie`): redact it to `Bearer ***`, or log a non-secret identifier instead — the token's row id or a short prefix of its hash — so support can still tell which token an integration sent. Scenario that fails as designed: every authenticated request writes its live bearer token at `info` level; anyone with access to the logs or the log pipeline (support, log aggregation vendor, a leaked log archive) replays it and acts as that user (CWE-532). Because every request goes through this one middleware, it also logs the credentials of every other authentication path that uses that header. Task 1.3 (`cargo test logs_requests`) should assert that the header value is absent from the log output.
findings.title: The middleware logs the Authorization header, writing every token to the logs

findings.recommendation: Revocation is deferred, and the design gives tokens no expiry and does not tie them to the password, so this change ships credentials that can never be turned off. Scenario: an integration's token leaks (the exact case the proposal's Why names — "a leaked integration exposes the account"); the user changes their password, which does not touch `api_tokens`, and the attacker keeps full API access indefinitely. Either bring a minimal revocation (delete a token by id, owned by the caller) into this change, or give tokens an expiry (`expires_at`, checked in the lookup), and in any case state in the Risks section what a user does when a token leaks. The current risk line only covers a lost token, not a leaked one.
findings.title: A leaked token cannot be invalidated by any means
